title: Using Set Learning to Improve Set-Valued Classifiers on Long-tailed Data
authors: Kevin Kasa, Scott C. Lowe, Graham W. Taylor
abstract: Set-valued classification (SVC) offers a practical approach to communicating uncertainty while maintaining accuracy by predicting variable-sized sets per input rather than fixed-sized sets (e.g. top-1 or top-5). However, set-valued classifiers (SVCs) exhibit significantly degraded performance on long-tailed and imbalanced datasets, a setting for which they are ostensibly well-suited. This becomes apparent under macro-average evaluation, which weighs all classes equally. SVCs are typically formed during a post-hoc calibration stage, so little is known about how training dynamics affect their behaviour. In this work, we investigate how different neural network training strategies and loss functions impact downstream SVC performance on highly imbalanced data. In addition to methods such as label smoothing and class-balancing, we investigate whether loss functions that operate over sets of examples in a batch, rather than treating all examples as independent, lead to better downstream SVCs. We adapt the recently proposed odd-K-out (OKO) loss function, which learns from sets of training samples, improving its sample efficiency whilst introducing algorithmic modifications that reduce its computational overhead from 3.2x to just 1.36x that of standard cross-entropy training. Experiments on highly long-tailed datasets demonstrate our modified OKO approach significantly improves macro-accuracy across multiple SVC methods - including top-k, average-k, and conformal prediction - while maintaining competitive micro-accuracy. This improved performance on minority classes occurs without substantially increasing prediction set sizes, suggesting that carefully constructed set-based training can produce networks better suited to imbalanced data.

title: Privacy-Preserving Robustness-Guided Testing
authors: Charles Koll, Houssam Abbas, Mike Rosulek
abstract: In industries like semi-conductors and aerospace, it is common for the design company to contract out part of the testing process to a Testing-as-a-Service (TaaS) company. In such a setup, both parties want to keep their intellectual property private (i.e. unknown to the other party): namely the design and its output traces for the designer, and the detailed correctness specifications for the tester. We demonstrate a practical way for conducting provably private TaaS using a cryptographically secure multi-party computation protocol. We do so for the common setup where the specification is in Signal Temporal Logic, and testing is done using robustness-guided falsification. Our implementation carefully separates the steps of falsification, and manages to be $\textit{maximally secure}$, in the sense that the parties learn the absolutely minimum necessary for falsification. For up to a 100-dimensional input search space, the generation of one test takes less than 80 msec, and the overhead of the privacy-preserving protocol is less than 6x. These numbers mean that privacy-preserving TaaS is practical, thus enabling TaaS in security-sensitive industries.

title: First pair coalescence among three geodesics
authors: Arjun Krishnan, Firas Rassoul-Agha, Timo Seppäläinen
abstract: In directed last-passage percolation with i.i.d. exponential vertex weights, the coalescence time $\operatorname{Coal}(a,b)$ of two semi-infinite geodesics started from vertices $a$ and $b$ in a fixed direction has a heavy tail with (KPZ) exponent $2/3$, and hence infinite expectation. We study instead the first coalescence among triples of semi-infinite geodesics in first- and last-passage percolation models (FPP/LPP) on $\mathbb{Z}^2$ that arise from stationary compatible families, such as Busemann geodesics. For directed FPP and LPP with arbitrary weights, we prove that $$\mathbb{E}\bigl[\min\{\operatorname{Coal}(a,a-e_1),\operatorname{Coal}(a,a-e_2)\}\bigr]<\infty.$$ We also consider FPP and LPP models in which antidiagonal motion is allowed, and prove that for every integer $k>0$, \[\mathbb{E}\bigl[\min\{\operatorname{Coal}(a,a-k(e_1-e_2)),\operatorname{Coal}(a,a+k(e_1-e_2))\}\bigr]<\infty.\] These results support the heuristic prediction that adjacent coalescence times are negatively associated.

title: Interflow: Breaking the Offline-Online Barrier for Private AI at the Edge
authors: Hanieh Totonchi Asl, Ebrahim Nouri, Zhuoran Li, Danella Zhao
abstract: Privacy-preserving machine learning (PPML) offers a promising path toward bringing powerful AI services to the edge without exposing sensitive user data. However, its practical deployment remains constrained by the high communication, computation, and data-movement costs of secure multi-party computation (MPC), particularly during nonlinear inference. Existing MPC systems typically decouple input-independent correlated randomness generation from online execution, creating substantial memory pressure to buffer single-use cryptographic data. Moreover, limited storage can force a stop-and-refill execution pattern that repeatedly stalls the pipeline to replenish these buffers, bringing randomness generation back onto the critical path. We propose Interflow, an algorithm-hardware co-design that rethinks this separation by batch-wise processing and pipelining correlated-randomness generation with online execution: while the current batch consumes pre-generated randomness to execute secure nonlinear operations, correlation generation proceeds concurrently for the next batch. By leveraging interleaved execution, efficient data movement, and hardware acceleration, the design transforms preprocessing from a serialized, storage-intensive offline phase into a continuously overlapped pipeline that generates correlated randomness closer to the point of consumption, reducing memory footprint and data movement overhead. Implemented on the Zynq UltraScale+ ZCU102, Interflow improves nonlinear evaluation throughput by up to 1.55x for CNN operators and 1.48x for transformer operators. It achieves up to 1.26x speedup for ResNet-50 and up to 1.21x speedup for BERT-base, and reduces memory footprint by up to 37%, compared with baseline frameworks.

title: Chiral magnetic excitations in the RMn6Sn6 kagome metals (R=Tb, Ho, Er, and Y)
authors: Christopher J. Ranlett, Tianxiong Han, S. X. M. Riberolles, Dhurba R. Jaishi, Tyler J. Slade, Bing Li, A. Sapkota, D. L. Abernathy, Rebecca L. Dally, J. W. Lynn, B. G. Ueland, R. J. McQueeney
abstract: Recent inelastic neutron scattering (INS) investigations of the kagome metal TbMn6Sn6 reveal novel chiral magnetic excitations associated with the kagome layer. These excitations appear to have an itinerant character with a large energy scale (> 100 meV) and heavy damping; however, the origin of these excitations, which are not predicted by local moment linear spin-wave theory, is not understood. Here, we use INS to show that chiral excitations are also found in RMn6Sn6 compounds with R=Tb, Ho, Er, and Y having uniaxial, tilted, planar ferrimagnet, and planar double-spiral magnetic structures, respectively. Thus, the chiral excitations exist regardless of the magnetic structure. Additionally, R=Er and Y demonstrate that the chiral mode intensity is weaker in planar magnetic structures, suggesting that excitations are transverse to the local Mn moment direction. The chiral excitations appear only at L=odd positions in the Brilloun zone, and correspond to chiral spin exciations of the same handedness within each kagome layer, and pi out-of-phase between layers.

title: In Situ Thermal Preparation by CO$_2$-Laser and Chemical Characterization of Oxide Substrates Across Multiple Crystallographic Orientations
authors: Neethu Rose Leyo, Sethulakshmi Sajeev, Arnaud P. Nono Tchiomo, Prosper Ngabonziza
abstract: Atomically flat and chemically controlled oxide substrate surfaces are essential for high-quality epitaxial growth of complex materials and heterostructures. Previous studies have demonstrated in situ thermal preparation of selected oxide substrates, primarily focusing on conventional low-index orientations such as SrTiO$_3$ (100) and LaAlO$_3$ (100). Here, we extend these methodologies to a broader range of oxide substrates and crystallographic orientations, including challenging polar surfaces. We present a systematic study of the in situ thermal preparation of SrTiO$_3$ (100), SrTiO$_3$ (111), GdScO$_3$ (110), LaAlO$_3$ (111), (LaAlO$_3$)$_{0.3}$(Sr$_2$AlTaO$_6$)$_{0.7}$ (001), and NdGaO$_3$ (110) single crystal substrates. The substrates are annealed in a vacuum chamber under a controlled oxygen background environment using a CO$_2$ laser heating system. The optimized annealing conditions produce atomically flat step-and-terrace structures, long-range surface crystallinity, and effectively clean surfaces across all the investigated substrates. Our results establish a versatile, reproducible, and broadly applicable platform for the in situ preparation of oxide substrates immediately prior to epitaxial growth. These results also provide practical guidelines for interface engineering and surface-sensitive investigations of complex materials.

title: Mixture of Censored Partially Linear Experts Models for Symmetric or Asymmetric Data with or without Outlying Observations: A novel approach with two-piece scale-mixture of normal distributions
authors: Mohsen Maleki, Geoffrey J. McLachlan
abstract: Finite mixture of partially linear model and finite mixture of experts models offer flexible tools for analyzing heterogeneous data, especially when covariates influence subgroup structure. Partially linear models further enhance this flexibility by combining linear and nonlinear effects. In many applications, however, censoring and departures from normality complicate estimation. To address these issues, we introduce a semiparametric mixture of censored partially linear expert models based on the two-piece scale mixture of normal family, which can accommodate skewness, heavy tails, and censoring. The proposed framework enables closed-form expressions in the E-step of an ECME algorithm, avoiding MCMC-based approximations and yielding stable maximum likelihood estimates. Simulation studies and real data analyses demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in settings with both heterogeneity and censoring.

title: Relational Complexity: Making Sense of Social Companion AI Use
authors: Sophie Elizabeth Klitgaard, Grace X. Wang, Daniel M. T. Fessler, Michelle H. Tang
abstract: The adoption of social companion AI (SCAI) is often framed in terms of the positive features it offers users, including its nonjudgemental nature, agreeableness, and availability. Here, we argue the appeal of these features primarily arises from the difficulties inherent in human sociality. SCAI reduces what we term relational complexity, or the demands and risks inherent in human relationships. Drawing insights from studies of human cognition, communication, and human-computer interaction, we identify six distinct sites of relational complexity that we posit are integral to understanding SCAI adoption. These include: (i) relationship formation and dissolution; (ii) achieving mutual understanding; (iii) interpersonal motives and strategic uncertainty; (iv) social partner evaluation and self-presentation; (v) social embeddedness and information flow; and (vi) reciprocity and relationship maintenance. By attenuating relational complexity, SCAI offers users some of the experiences associated with companionship while reducing the demands intrinsic to obtaining such experiences from another person. However, the lower interpersonal risk and diminished cognitive load that attracts users to SCAI may contribute to myriad negative impacts, including relationship displacement, social demotivation, social deskilling, and risks to privacy. The concept of relational complexity thus provides a framework for studying both the appeal of artificial companionship and its implications for human wellbeing.

title: KPHarness: Co-Evolving Knowledge and Probing for Long-Horizon Gaming Harnesses
authors: Zhikang Chen, Yueqing Sun, Sen Cui, Ziang Ye, Yu Wang, Yan Feng2, Xierui Song, Yu Zhang, Tingting Zhu
abstract: A failed gaming trajectory reveals that an agent needs intervention, but not necessarily how its execution harness should change. Effective harness adaptation therefore requires gathering diagnostic evidence, rather than merely proposing alternative recovery rules. We present KPHarness, a framework that adapts the external execution harness of a frozen vision-language-action model through knowledge-probing co-evolution. Recovery knowledge supplies context-specific intervention hypotheses that guide active probing; probe outcomes reveal when these hypotheses apply and provide evidence for refining both recovery knowledge and later probe selection. This reciprocal process allows the harness to improve not only which interventions it applies, but also how it investigates failures. KPHarness separates fast policy execution from a slow research loop that translates accumulated knowledge and probing evidence into bounded harness revisions. Each revision is compared with the incumbent under matched sandbox conditions and accepted only when the paired evaluation shows improvement. Recoveries supported by further validation are retained for cross-task reuse, while immediate interaction feedback and delayed episode-success credit update action- and knowledge-probing policies during adaptation. Experiments on Minecraft tasks spanning mining, combat, and crafting show improved task coverage over bare policy execution, a manually specified fixed harness, and knowledge-only harness evolution with non-adaptive probing. Evaluation on previously unseen tasks further shows improved task completion with the evolved harness, knowledge bank, and probing policies held fixed,

title: Real-Time Disturbance-Aware Koopman Model Predictive Control for Quadrotors in Spatially Varying Winds
authors: Stella Kombo, Masih Haseli, Alejandro A. Stefan-Zavala, Peter I. Renn, Morteza Gharib, Joel W. Burdick
abstract: Reliable quadrotor flight in disturbed environments requires predictive models that remain accurate as unmodeled aerodynamic effects change during deployment. We introduce a disturbance-aware Koopman Control Family (DA-KCF) framework that preserves an offline-identified nominal model while learning only a disturbance-induced correction online. A reference-dependent KCF is first learned from simulation data and calibrated using limited hardware data. During deployment, the nominal KCF remains fixed while a lightweight residual ensemble learns a low-dimensional disturbance correction from causal state-command-state transitions. The Adaptive DA-KCF model is incorporated into MPC, where disturbance corrections are evaluated along the prediction horizon to optimize position and yaw references sent to the onboard stabilizing controller. Hardware experiments on a nano-quadrotor under uniform wind and a spatially varying wake demonstrate that online adaptation improves multi-step prediction and trajectory tracking as disturbance-induced model mismatch increases, while satisfying real-time control requirements.

title: Linear Preservers of Semipositivity over Proper Cones
authors: Yulong Tian, Jinli Xu
abstract: We classify all real linear operators on $M_{m,n}(\mathbb{R})$, with $m,n\ge2$, that preserve semipositivity between two prescribed pairs of proper cones, without assuming invertibility. Every such operator has product form $L(A)=XAY$ or degenerate form $L(A)=Ψ(u^TA)$, possibly both. We give necessary and sufficient cone conditions for each form; the degenerate condition is expressed through a linear matrix pencil on the dual of the target output cone. The degenerate preservers are exactly those of operator rank $n$, and every preserver of larger rank has product form. We also classify all linear preservers from $M_{2,2}(\mathbb{R})$ to $M_{1,3}(\mathbb{R})$ over the nonnegative orthants, obtaining three disjoint classes, including two rank-three classes outside product form.

title: Structural equation modelling--based meta-analytic model for diagnostic test accuracy studies
authors: Zelalem F. Negeri
abstract: Bivariate random-effects models are commonly used to jointly synthesize sensitivity and specificity in diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) meta-analysis. However, existing approaches may be sensitive to distributional assumptions and may produce biased estimates of accuracy and between-study heterogeneity with sparse meta-analytic data. We proposed a novel bivariate structural equation modelling (BSEM) approach for DTA meta-analysis and evaluated its performance relative to the bivariate linear mixed model (BLMM) and bivariate generalized linear mixed model (BGLMM). We conducted extensive simulations under varying study, sample-size, accuracy, and heterogeneity conditions. We assessed model performance using bias, root mean squared error (RMSE), confidence interval width, empirical 95% coverage probability (CP), and convergence. We generated study-specific random effects from bivariate normal, t, and Laplace distributions to assess robustness to distributional misspecification. We also applied the models to two empirical DTA datasets. The BSEM generally produced smaller bias and RMSE and nominal-level CP for pooled sensitivity and specificity than the BLMM, while the BGLMM generally yielded results between the two approaches. The BLMM showed stable convergence but tended to underestimate between-study heterogeneity. We observed similar performance patterns under the three random-effects distributions. In the empirical applications, differences between model estimates were generally consistent with patterns observed in the simulations. Overall, the proposed BSEM provided a flexible alternative approach for jointly modelling sensitivity and specificity in DTA meta-analysis, with performance that was generally favourable relative to the BLMM and comparable to the BGLMM across the simulated and empirical settings considered.

title: The environments of type Ibn supernovae: evidence for a strong Wolf-Rayet star component
authors: Timo Kravtsov, Hanindyo Kuncarayakti, Joseph P. Anderson
abstract: Characterisation of progenitor stars of supernovae (SNe) poses several challenges. Direct observations of progenitors are based on serendipitious archival observations and are only possible for nearby events. Indirect methods include inferring nickel mass from the light curves or oxygen masses from the SN's nebular phase, both of which are tools to constrain the progenitor's initial mass. Alternatively, environments of SNe have been used as a proxy for the progenitor's age and metallicity. The progenitor channel of type Ibn SNe is a hotly debated topic. The mass-loss and the formation of He-rich circumstellar medium requires strong envelope stripping of the progenitor star. For core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe), this requires strong stellar wind mass losses, i.e. a Wolf-Rayet (WR) star, or binary interaction with a companion star. Here, we analyse a sample of host galaxies of type Ibn SNe that have been observed with MUSE. We use H$α$ emission to infer the transient's association to star formation and derive the local metallicity with commonly used strong line diagnostic. We find that the sample of SNe are highly associated with star formation in the host galaxy, typically situated within one of the brightest HII regions in the host galaxy. The NCR distribution of H$α$ pixels in SN Ibn environments strongly resembles that of WR stars, and shows a stronger preference to SF compared to other core-collapse SN types. Metallicity measurements show typically sub-solar metallicity in the SN environments.

title: Constant-Depth Quantum Barrier Option Pricing via a Static Bivariate Oracle Framework
authors: Ji-Hui Mo, Yuan-Hong Tao
abstract: Quantum amplitude estimation offers a theoretical quadratic speedup over classical Monte Carlo methods for financial derivative pricing. However, extending gate-based algorithms to path-dependent barrier options has historically been hampered by sequential path discretization, where tracking price paths across $d$ monitoring dates incurs a linear escalation in qubit footprint and gate depth ($\mathcal{O}(d)$), posing severe coherence challenges for near-term quantum processors. In this work, we present a constant-depth quantum pricing framework that fundamentally eliminates the temporal dependency of barrier monitoring. Leveraging the Brownian reflection principle and Girsanov theorem, we project the continuous supremum dynamics onto a static bivariate joint distribution of the terminal price $S_T$ and running supremum $M_T$. This allows decoupling dynamic boundary checks into a static bivariate oracle comprising two parallel comparators and a dual-controlled rotation gate. We prove this architecture reduces circuit depth and comparator complexity from $\mathcal{O}(d)$ to an invariant $\mathcal{O}(1)$, while supporting discrete monitoring via zero-quantum-cost boundary corrections. Transpilation benchmarks for daily monitoring ($d = 252$) show our framework slashes physical CNOT count by 98.59% (from 2262 to 32) and compresses two-qubit depth by 98.02% (from 1514 to 30 layers). Under a realistic 127-qubit IBM Eagle noise model, the shallow circuit achieves a 7.84% relative valuation error with M3 readout mitigation. Finally, the framework seamlessly extends to nonlinear exotic payoffs lacking analytical solutions, establishing a noise-resilient pathway toward practical quantum advantage in computational finance.

title: Why Do LLMs Accept Generics? Explaining Acceptability using Psycholinguistic and Model-Derived Factors
authors: Mervat Abassy, Zhaoxin Feng, Tatsuki Kuribayashi, Kentaro Inui, Emmanuele Chersoni
abstract: Psycholinguistic studies explore why humans accept some generic statements but reject others by showing that these judgments depend on more than how common a property is. People consider several other factors such as how well it sets the kind apart from others or whether it is characteristic of the kind. Inspired by the linguistic and cognitive literature, we explore to what extent factors from these studies explain how large language models (LLMs) judge generics. Our results with twelve models on a psycholinguistic dataset and on naturally occurring generics show that models weigh how common a property is against how well it distinguishes the kind, and combine the two much as people do, though less clearly. Like people, they favor characteristic properties, but unlike the accounts of human judgment, they ignore striking ones. What matters most to LLMs is whether a statement is factually true, and much of the influence of human factors reaches their ratings through that judgment. In six 7-9B models, shifting the hidden states along each factor's direction moves the judgment as the factor predicts.

title: Schrödinger estimates with arbitrarily small periodic regularity on $\mathbb{H}^2 \times \mathbb{T}$
authors: Xuyi Wei
abstract: Let $M=\mathbb{H}^2\times\mathbb{T}$ carry its product metric. We prove that the Schrödinger evolution maps $L^2(\mathbb{H}^2;H^s(\mathbb{T}))$ into $L^2([0,1];L^6(M))$ for every $s>0$, without any regularity assumption in the hyperbolic variable. The proof separates hyperbolic and periodic frequencies. A localized hyperbolic kernel estimate restricts the effective interaction time at hyperbolic frequency $L$ to order $L^{-1}$. Quadratic exponential sums then give a logarithmic bound when the periodic bandwidth is comparable to $L$. A mixed-norm decoupling argument, including an $L^6$-valued extension and a periodic transference step, reduces wider periodic bands to this case. The infimum of the admissible periodic regularities is therefore zero. The estimate at zero regularity is not established here.

title: SPAR: Stepwise Personalized Autoregressive Recommendation with Prefix-Balanced Semantic IDs
authors: Chunrui Zhang, Gaoyun Lin, Chang Zhou, Zheng Hu, Qiran Song, Shimin Cai, Tao Zhou
abstract: Semantic ID (SID)-based generative recommendation retrieves items through successive token-level decisions, making personalization at each decoding step essential. However, existing methods insufficiently account for prefix-dependent user evidence and imbalanced historical interaction loads among candidate branches. This can cause irreversible branch-selection errors and favor popular paths. We propose SPAR, a generative recommendation framework that jointly improves stepwise personalization and SID construction. Its PATH Decoder retrieves prefix-relevant evidence from compressed long-term user memories and combines it with recent behavior, user profiles, and event context to guide each token decision. Its RQ-PIB module balances historical interaction loads among sibling branches under each parent prefix while preserving semantic structure. Experiments on large-scale Youku production data show an average relative HitRate improvement of 2.66% over the strongest baseline. SPAR also increases target-prefix retention by 5.79 percentage points and reduces the traffic-weighted largest child-branch share by 32.84% across SID levels. In a 7-day online A/B test, SPAR serves 10% of Youku's production traffic and improves average watch time per user by 3.95% and play conversion rate by 3.38%. These results demonstrate more reliable hierarchical decoding, balanced SID branches, and improved user engagement in industrial recommendation.

title: Gaze2HOI: Gaze-Aware Intention Disambiguation for Egocentric Hand-Object Interaction Forecasting
authors: Chuanyang Ma, Chenye Wang, Yixuan Wang, Huiling Zhou, Xingqun Qi, Muyi Sun, Man Zhang, Caifeng Shan, Zhenan Sun
abstract: Anticipating how users will interact with their surroundings is essential for proactive systems that provide timely assistance in AR, VR, and embodied applications. Prior work typically forecasts hand-object interactions directly from historical observations, leaving intention and contact geometry implicit. However, similar observation histories can precede semantically or geometrically distinct futures. Inspired by behavioral evidence that gaze can provide early cues for underlying intention, we propose Gaze2HOI, a gaze-aware framework that formulates hand-object interaction forecasting as a hierarchical problem comprising intention inference, contact grounding, and coupled hand-object motion generation. Specifically, Gaze2HOI first weights gaze cues by fixation strength and recency, and uses them to modulate the visual representations of a vision-language model (VLM) through Temporal Gaze Saliency Modulation (TGSM), thereby reducing semantic ambiguity in intention inference. Subsequently, an Anticipatory Contact Grounding (ACG) module maps these structured intentions into explicit contact, support, and placement fields, effectively mitigating geometric ambiguity. Driven by these explicit conditions, a diffusion-based model jointly generates the 6-DoF object trajectories and future articulated motion of both hands. To evaluate Gaze2HOI, we further introduce EgoAIM, a phase-aware benchmark that organizes egocentric hand-object interactions into four phases defined by evolving hand-object relations and provides fine-grained intention annotations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Gaze2HOI achieves state-of-the-art performance in both intention inference and motion forecasting, even approaching oracle-level end-to-end performance in specific interaction phases. Project page: https://gaze2hoi.github.io/.

title: Classification of positive solutions to the critical Lane-Emden system
authors: Yuxia Guo, Yichen Hu, Shaolong Peng, Tingfeng Yuan
abstract: We classify all positive classical solutions of the Lane--Emden system $$ -Δu=v^p \, \, \text{in } \, \, \mathbb{R}^N, \, \, -Δv=u^q \, \, \text{in} \, \, \mathbb{R}^N, $$ where $N\geq3$ and $p,q>0$ satisfy $$ \frac{1}{p+1}+\frac{1}{q+1}=\frac{N-2}{N}.$$Without assuming boundedness, decay at infinity, or finite energy, we prove that every such solution has the form $$ u(x)=λ^{\frac{N}{q+1}}U(λ(x-a)), \, \, v(x)=λ^{\frac{N}{p+1}}V(λ(x-a)), $$ for some $a\in \mathbb{R}^N$ and $λ>0$, where $(U,V)$ is the positive radial ground state centered at the origin and normalized by $U(0)=1$. Consequently, both components are radially symmetric about the same point and satisfy $$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}u^{q+1}\, dx = \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}v^{p+1}\,dx<\infty. $$ Our result extends the classical classification of positive solutions of the critical Sobolev equation by Caffarelli, Gidas and Spruck and Chen and Li to the critical Lane-Emden system.

title: Inverse domain uncertainty quantification in hemodynamics: sampling virtual patient cohorts under constraints
authors: Francesco Romor, Jose Rodrigo Rojo-Garcia, André-Alexander Zepernick, Ana Djurdjevac, Alfonso Caiazzo
abstract: We consider the following inverse domain uncertainty quantification problem: given a prescribed value or measurement of a hemodynamic biomarker, characterize the distribution of vascular geometries compatible with it. The problem is formulated as a Bayesian inverse problem in which a high-dimensional latent parameter encodes the cardiovascular shape and accounts for inter-patient variability. The parameter-to-observable map composes a conditional LDDMM stochastic interpolant generating the aortic surface with a high-performance numerical finite element solver for the unsteady incompressible Navier--Stokes equations, from which biomarkers of interest are evaluated. The map is nonlinear, high-dimensional and computationally expensive. To address the problem, we compare three ensemble strategies: ensemble adjusted Kalman inversion (EAKI), adaptive Bayesian updating with structural reliability (aBUS), and a Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao (WFR) sequential Monte Carlo scheme. The first two approaches are derivative-free. For the third method, we introduce a novel differentiable flow-matching surrogate that reduces the cost of a single forward map evaluation at the price of a distribution shift depending on the training distribution used for the surrogate. We apply the framework to the generation of virtual patient cohorts matching prescribed pressure drops along aortic geometries affected by coarctation, and we validate and compare the three methods on synthetic data.

title: VISH-ASR: Viterbi-Guided Selection of Hotwords for Speech-LLM Contextual ASR
authors: Xiaoyu Gu, Yu Xi, Chencheng Wang, Zonghan Zhou, Haoyu Li, Jing Peng, Kai Yu
abstract: Prompt-based contextual ASR requires selecting a compact hotword subset from large dynamic inventories, yet existing pre-selection methods rely either on discrete ASR hypotheses that may discard acoustic evidence or on separately trained retrieval models. We propose Viterbi-guided Selection of Hotwords (VISH), a training-free, plug-and-play framework that directly verifies candidate-specific acoustic support over frame-level CTC posteriors. VISH formulates pre-selection as constrained posterior search; M-VISH makes large-list verification scalable through frame-synchronous shared-prefix Viterbi search with bounded top-K pruning, while Bi-MVISH exploits complementary backward evidence for robust verification. Across five benchmarks, M-VISH achieves up to 11.7% absolute improvement in Best-F1 over a strong learned-retrieval baseline and reduces candidate-search latency by 75.2% at 2,000 candidates relative to hypothesis-based filtering. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of posterior-level verification for accurate and scalable hotword pre-selection without additional model training.

title: From Tokens to Files: Multi-Granularity Detection and Localization of AI-Involved Code
authors: Yue Xu, Xiyang Wang, Hui Liu, Bolei He
abstract: The increasing use of large language models for code generation calls for methods that distinguish purely human-written code from AI-involved code: files in which any part, however small, was generated or substantially modified by a model. Beyond flagging such files, we aim to localize the lines or blocks attributable to AI. Existing approaches compress a file into a single score, from surface stylistic features or a global code representation, which averages away the evidence when only a few blocks are AI-involved. We propose a framework that models AI authorship at the token level and predicts at the line, block, and file levels. A frozen code language model is equipped with two low-rank adapters, trained separately on machine-written and human-written files; their per-token log-likelihood ratio provides local evidence of AI authorship. Lightweight heads aggregate this evidence within lines and blocks, using the surrounding code context, and their local predictions are aggregated into a file-level decision. We train on mixed-authorship files built from human originals and their AI-generated or AI-modified counterparts, including continuation and fill-in-the-middle scenarios. On an internal test set of 11,773 AI-involved files across six generation regimes against 2,541 human files, our method reaches 72.4 macro F1 at a 1% FPR operating point. With no adaptation, it reaches 62.5 line-level F1 on HybridCodeAuthorship, an external human-AI co-writing benchmark with no training split, above the 56 its own paper reports as the best line-level result. On 19,445 human-written files from repositories created before 2022, the false-positive rate stays between 0.55% and 0.81% under the transported 1% threshold, so the operating point holds on real human code.

title: RoboCasa-Shift: Stage-Aware Robustness Evaluation of Vision-Language-Action Policies in Long-Horizon Household Manipulation
authors: Haocheng Wang, Youquan Liu, Weiyu Guo, Aokai Zhang, Donghang Wu, Hongyu Liu, Sha Zhang, Weidong Yang, Ben Fei
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) robustness is commonly summarized by aggregate task success, which obscures how individual executions change under distribution shifts and where failures emerge in long-horizon tasks. We introduce \textbf{RoboCasa-Shift}, a diagnostic robustness benchmark built on RoboCasa365 that combines controlled single-factor shifts, matched clean-perturbed rollouts in which each pair shares the same underlying settings and differs only in the target shift, and simulator-grounded stage-aware diagnostics. We evaluate GR00T N1.5 on four long-horizon tasks that pass a predefined clean-performance gate under four perturbation factors and three calibrated severity levels, including conditions that drive the evaluated policy to complete task failure, totaling 1,040 formal rollouts. Robustness responses vary substantially across factors and tasks, and increasing severity does not always produce monotonic degradation. For example, one camera condition yields $Δ\mathrm{SR}=0$ despite 8 of 80 matched episodes changing outcome. Stage-aware analysis further shows that the same end-to-end degradation can correspond to different execution-depth profiles. Camera $L_2$ and Gaussian blur $L_1$ both yield $Δ\mathrm{SR}=0.188$, yet their first-stage failure rates are 19.0\% and 36.4\%, respectively. Our findings suggest that VLA robustness should be viewed as a multi-dimensional property of execution rather than a single end-to-end performance measure, motivating evaluation protocols that jointly capture outcome degradation, paired outcome sensitivity, and failure progression. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/HaochengWang23/RoboCasa-Shift.

title: Classical-to-Quantum Transition in Blackbody Radiation Thermodynamics: Planck's Law without Statistical Assumptions
authors: J. Wang, G. Casati, G. Benenti
abstract: Inspired by Fermi's model of radiation-matter interaction, we investigate the classical dynamics of a closed, finite-energy system, in which matter is coupled to an electromagnetic field. We find that energy is progressively transferred to increasingly high-frequency field modes, so that the effective temperature of both matter and radiation approaches zero in the long-time limit - in sharp contradiction with the finite-temperature equilibrium assumed by classical blackbody thermodynamics. Requiring consistency with the Stefan-Boltzmann and Wien laws identifies a characteristic time $t_L$, at which both laws are simultaneously satisfied. Strikingly, classical spectra obtained for different energies and cavity sizes collapse onto the universal Planck distribution at $t_L$. We conjecture that quantum dynamical localization arrests the classical energy cascade at $t_L$, and that the Planck distribution emerges as a dynamical consequence of this arrest - without invoking any a priori statistical assumption.

title: The Lévy-Khinchine type representations and generalized functions on Bernstein spaces
authors: A. A. Khartov
abstract: We consider the class of all univariate probability laws whose characteristic functions do not have zeroes on the real line. This class contains the fundamental family of infinitely divisible distributions and its new extension, the set of rational-(quasi-)infinitely divisible laws. We prove that this class is dense in the family of all probability laws with respect to the total variation distance. We show that characteristic functions corresponding to this class admit Lévy-Khinchine type representations. In these formulas, the generalized spectral functions (the regularized Lévy measures) are special continuous linear functionals on the union of well known Bernstein spaces of entire functions of exponential type which are additionally bounded on the real line. We apply this spectral functions in criteria of weak convergence of distributions within the class under study. All necessary analytical constructions are proposed.

title: Flavor decomposition of electromagnetic multipole moments in $[q_1q_2][\bar q_3 \bar c]$ tetraquarks: Light-quark analogs of $T_{cs1}(2900)^0$ with $J^P = 1^+$
authors: Ulaş Özdem
abstract: We present a systematic study of the magnetic dipole and electric quadrupole moments of compact $[q_1 q_2][\bar q_3 \bar c]$ tetraquark states with quantum numbers $J^P = 1^+$, in the diquark--antidiquark picture and within the light-cone QCD sum rule framework. By performing a flavor decomposition across all admissible $u/d$ configurations, we show that the charm-quark contribution to the electromagnetic moments vanishes algebraically at the operator level -- a structural feature of the specific spin organization adopted here, in which the heavy antiquark resides in a pseudoscalar antidiquark, distinct from the dynamical $1/m_c$ suppression operative in alternative compact constructions and in hadronic molecules. The magnetic moments follow a coherent light-flavor pattern -- positive for $uu$-, negative for $dd$-, and suppressed for mixed-flavor diquarks -- and the quadrupole moments are non-zero throughout, corresponding, in the customary geometrical interpretation, to intrinsically deformed charge distributions. We further identify the dimensionless multipole ratio $\mathcal{D}/μ$ as a structural observable, independent of the normalization of the interpolating current, which probes the relative geometry of the spin-current and charge distributions complementary to the absolute moments. Taken together, the algebraic decoupling of the charm contribution and the operator-level distinction it implies among different singly-heavy tetraquark architectures constitute methodological signatures that discriminate among the corresponding internal organizations and, to the extent that a physical candidate is dominated by one of them, among compact and molecular interpretations.

title: Primes in short intervals assuming the Riemann hypothesis
authors: Matt Visser
abstract: In 2001 Baker, Harman, and Pintz proved, for $x$ sufficiently large, the existence of at least one prime in the sub-linear interval $[x,x+x^{\frac{1}{2} +\frac{1}{40}}]$. But just how large is sufficiently large? In the current note I shall make the Baker--Harman--Pintz theorem effective, but at an extremely high price. Contingent upon assuming validity of the Riemann hypothesis (RH), I shall show that the Baker--Harman--Pintz theorem holds for $x \geq 3.5\times 10^{90}$. Furthermore, again assuming RH, I shall also show that for any $0< m\leq15.831$ and $x \geq 1$ there is at least one prime in the interval $[x,x+x^{\frac{1}{2} +\frac{1}{m}}]$, and that for $M\geq 2.29$ and $y \geq 1$ there is at least one prime in the interval $[y^M, (y+1)^M]$.

title: Raise or Check? Predicting the Necessity of Additional Fuzzing for Continuous Fuzzing
authors: Riku Kato, Tatsuya Shirai, Olivier Nourry, Yutaro Kashiwa, Kenji Fujiwara, Yasutaka Kamei, Hajimu Iida
abstract: Continuous fuzzing is used for vulnerability detection in Open Source Software (OSS). Large-scale services such as Google's OSS-Fuzz fuzz over 1,300 projects and have revealed more than 10,000 vulnerabilities. Despite this, a considerable time lag often exists between when a vulnerability is introduced and when it is detected (i.e., the window of exposure). Given the computational cost of additional fuzzing, we aim to allocate fuzzing resources efficiently using vulnerability-risk estimates. We propose RAISE (Risk-Aware Intensive Supplemental Execution Framework), a Just-In-Time (JIT) framework that prioritizes additional fuzzing for high-risk project-days. RAISE performs binary classification at the project-day granularity to estimate whether a vulnerability is introduced on a given day. We construct a dataset combining vulnerability-introducing commits from the OSV database with daily coverage and change metrics from OSS-Fuzz, covering 15 C/C++ projects and 15,210 project-days, of which 347 (2.28%) are vulnerability-introducing. In a cross-project validation setting, our best model, a Random Forest combining VCCFinder-based static features with dynamic fuzzing features, achieves a ROC-AUC of 0.74, substantially outperforming a random baseline; coverage metrics, led by PatchCoverage, are the most important features. In a simulation over 968 vulnerabilities comparing five allocation strategies, Simple-Regression was significantly more cost-efficient than the prediction-agnostic heuristics, spending 91.60 additional fuzzing sessions per detected vulnerability, roughly half the cost of the Median heuristic (171.89). RAISE shows that JIT vulnerability prediction with coverage-aware fuzzing features can effectively guide risk-aware allocation of continuous fuzzing resources.

title: The Dimension Landscape of Bivariate $C^2$ Splines
authors: Xinyu Wu, Jiansong Deng
abstract: Schumaker's lower bound incorporates local geometric corrections and provides insight into the dimensions of bivariate spline spaces. Building on this bound, we study bivariate $C^2$ spline dimensions from three perspectives: universal attainment, generic attainment, and geometric jumps. We prove universal attainment in degree seven for every legal realization of every triangulation. We prove generic attainment in degrees five and six for every fixed combinatorial triangulation and give explicit polynomial conditions certifying generic failure on fixed triangulations in degrees three and four. For geometric jumps with matching local direction types at corresponding interior vertices, we prove nonexistence in degree seven and construct examples in degrees three and five. In degree six, universal attainment and the existence of such geometric jumps remain open questions.

title: SliMOO: Interpretable Multi-Objective Evolutionary Search for LLM Depth Pruning
authors: Guanchen Li, Yixing Xu, Xuanwu Yin, Dong Li, Emad Barsoum
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) grow more powerful, their scale makes them costly to serve. Depth pruning offers a practical route to efficiency by directly reducing memory and latency without hardware-specific support. However, we observe that transformer layers exhibit markedly different task-dependent layer contributions, whereas existing depth-pruning methods ignore this heterogeneity and thus tend to optimize for a narrow domain or benchmark rather than preserve broad capability. This suggests that LLM depth pruning should be formulated as a multi-objective optimization problem rather than a single-score ranking problem. We propose SliMOO, an interpretable multi-objective evolutionary search framework for LLM depth pruning. SliMOO first uses single-layer removal probing to construct a task-layer importance map, which provides an interpretable view of task-shared and task-specific layers and serves as a search prior. It then performs a Pareto-aware evolutionary search for pruning masks, where candidates are generated under the guidance of the task-layer prior, scored by their deviation from the dense model on each task, and retained through NSGA-II environmental selection. Across the Llama-3.1 and Qwen3 model families, SliMOO consistently achieves stronger multi-task trade-offs than rule-based, greedy, and scalarized baselines. For example, on Llama-3.1-70B at 25% sparsity, it improves the math-domain average from 24.33% to 34.40% and the code-domain average from 35.03% to 39.14%. Code will be made available at https://github.com/AMD-AGI/SliMOO.

title: Probing the Optical/UV Continuum Variability of Active Galactic Nuclei with the Damped Random Walk Model
authors: Xiang-Wei Ning, Wen-Jie Hu, Zi-Han Yuan, Yi Tang, Yan-Song Ma, Yu-Meng Gua, Le-Yi Huang, Wei-Hao Bian
abstract: Optical/UV continuum variability over baselines of up to 20 yr is investigated using the damped random walk (DRW) model for 1214 active galactic nuclei (AGNs) compiled from Y. Shen et al. and C. J. Burke et al. Among these, 115 AGNs with reliable DRW fitting and unbiased DRW parameters (timescale $τ_{2500}$ and amplitude $σ_{2500}$ at the rest-frame 2500~Å) are used to examine the relations between the variability and the accretion properties. We found a significant correlation of $τ_{2500}$ with black hole mass ($M_{\rm BH}$) and dimensionless accretion rate ($\dot{\mathscr{M}}$) of the form $τ_{2500} \propto M_{\rm BH}^{0.50\pm0.07} \dot{\mathscr{M}}^{0.27\pm0.04}$, while the dependence on the continuum luminosity at 5100~Å and redshift becomes insignificant after controlling for $M_{\rm BH}$. $τ_{2500}$ also correlate with the mass accretion rate ($\dot{M}$) as $τ_{2500} \propto \dot{M}^{0.41\pm0.04}$, which is consistent with the thermal timescale expected from the standard thin-disk model within $3σ$ uncertainties; while the average value is consistent with the expectations of the model, the scatter in the relation can be due to differences in the viscosity parameter ($α$) or in disk temperature profiles. Assuming that \tauuv\ corresponds to the accretion disk thermal timescale, the disk-emitting radius at rest-frame 2500~Å ($R_{2500}$) is found to correlate with $M_{\rm BH}$ as $R_{2500} \propto M_{\rm BH}^{0.53\pm0.05}$. Using the microlensing-based $R_{2500}-M_{\rm BH}$ relation of C. W. Morgan et al., $α$ is statistically estimated to be $0.04\pm0.01$.

title: Collective Hall quantization in 3D Chern vector systems
authors: Zhi-Qiang Zhang, Shuguang Cheng, Hongfang Liu, Hailong Li, Hua Jiang, X. C. Xie
abstract: Understanding the three-dimensional (3D) quantum Hall effect, characterized by a Chern vector rather than a single Chern number, has been a central pursuit in topological physics. While quantized Hall transport is established for the special case with one nonzero Chern component, recent realizations of more general Chern-vector states raise a fundamental question: how does such topology protect quantized transport? Here, we predict a distinct 3D quantized Hall effect protected by $\mathbf{C}=(0,m,n)$. For samples with dimensions $L_y$ and $L_z$, global topology enforces collective quantization of $mL_y+nL_z$, despite the fragility of individual edge modes to disorder. This reveals a novel transport regime in which robust quantization emerges as a holistic property of a unified chiral network,rather than of its constituent modes. Crucially, this collective response manifests as a quantized Hall conductance $G_{xy}=\pm(mL_y+nL_z)e^2/h$, with a distinctive dependence on both Chern-vector components and sample dimensions. We propose candidate materials to facilitate experimental observation.

title: Absolute winning properties of exceptional sets for rational maps
authors: Haoyang Ji
abstract: We study Schmidt's game on the Julia set $J(f)$ of weak hyperbolic rational maps $f:\CC\to\CC$. For each $y\in J(f)$, let $E(f,y)$ be the set of points in $J(f)$ whose forward orbits stay a positive distance from $y$. We prove that $E(f,y)$ is absolute winning on $J(f)$ for each $y \in J(f)$. To do this, we first prove the absolute winning property for the exceptional set associated to the critical points by a potential game argument, and then use uniform expansion to obtain the result for each target point $y$.

title: Narrowband nonreciprocal transmission in a Doppler-broadened multilevel atomic system
authors: Ying-Xue Zhang, Hui-Min Zhao, Yan-Kui Bai
abstract: We theoretically investigate narrowband nonreciprocal transmission in a Doppler-broadened five-level M-type atomic medium. After Doppler averaging, the M-type system retains a narrow near-resonant electromagnetically induced transparency window that is narrower than that of a standard three-level $Λ$ system. This spectral narrowing is associated with the decreasing separation between the two inner dressed states as atomic velocity increases. The transparency window exhibits pronounced direction-dependent transmission, with high forward transmission and strong suppression in the reverse direction. The transparency linewidth and forward-backward probe transmission can be controlled via two independent driving fields, while the central transparency frequency is kept essentially unchanged. The resulting narrowband nonreciprocity supports high forward transmission together with strong suppression in the reverse direction, which is suitable for frequency-selective optical filtering and nonreciprocal optical transmission in thermal atomic media. Our scheme with these specific features is geared towards enabling compact vapor-cell-based nonreciprocal devices for quantum network applications.

title: Suppression and reemergence of directional transport across the ferromagnetic transition in SrRuO$_3$
authors: Smriti Bhatia, Neha Sharma, Srishti Bhardwaj, Shruti Roy, Dirk Fuchs, Tulika Maitra, Vivek Kumar Malik, Kaushik Sen
abstract: SrRuO$_3$ is a canonical itinerant ferromagnet that continues to serve as a fertile platform for exploring spin-orbit coupled transport and topological responses in correlated oxide metals. Here, we investigate a (110)-oriented epitaxial SrRuO3 thin film on DyScO$_3$, where crystallographic anisotropy allows for symmetry-resolved charge transport along orthogonal in-plane directions. We uncover two principal findings. First, the resistance above the Curie temperature $T_{c,on}\approx 165$ K exhibits strong anisotropy, consistent with directionally dependent spin-fluctuation scattering. Below $T_{c,on}$, this anisotropy nearly vanishes, despite persistent structural inequivalence, due to isotropic electron-magnon and electron-electron scattering processes. Second, the application of a magnetic field reveals a striking directional contrast in the linear magnetoresistance (MR): it remains negative and saturates along [001], but changes sign and becomes positive along $[1\bar{1}0]$ below $T_0=145$ K. In contrast, the quadratic MR term is identical for both directions and peaks near $T_{\mathrm{OHE}}^*=155$ K, where the ordinary Hall coefficient crosses zero, consistent with carrier compensation under a two-band scenario. A sign change in the anomalous Hall signal at $T_{\mathrm{AHE}}^*=150$ K is consistent with a temperature-dependent redistribution of Berry-curvature contributions near the Fermi level. These results establish ferromagnetic ordering as the primary driver of the observed directional magnetotransport in SrRuO$_3$.

title: Are Linguistic and Arithmetic Circuits Dissociated in LLMs?
authors: Riku Kisako, Tatsuki Kuribayashi, Ryohei Sasano
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit both knowledge of language, rendered by, for example, grammatical judgment ability, and abilities to perform tasks through language, such as math-word problem solving. Motivated by neurolinguistic studies of their neural dissociation in human brains, in this study, we investigate the overlap of their circuits in large language models (LLMs). Specifically, we examine the overlap and causal effects between the circuits extracted for linguistic and arithmetic tasks, using controlled materials and circuit discovery methods from the mechanistic interpretability field. Our experiments with five LLMs show that circuit similarity is mostly explained by task domains (linguistic vs. arithmetic), rather than by their input and output vocabularies or by the syntactic similarities between natural-language sentences and arithmetic expressions. This finding suggests that LLMs may process linguistic and arithmetic information using largely separate neural circuits, highlighting an ability-based modular organization of circuits within these models.

title: Foundations of the Scaling Law
authors: Tianyu Zhao, Zhixiang Ren
abstract: Empirical scaling laws relate validation loss to model size, training exposure and compute, providing a quantitative basis for allocating resources. This technical note explains these relationships through three linked analyses. Geometric approximation connects spatial resolution, intrinsic dimension and smoothness to function error; the loss function determines how that error transfers to task risk. Spectral analysis combines feature visibility, covariance eigenvalues and target alignment to describe how additional data reduce unresolved predictive mass. Constrained optimization then gives the parameter-data balance and the training-inference trade-off. We also examine emergence and grokking, separating scoring thresholds from learning dynamics, and test-time scaling, separating candidate coverage from selected-answer accuracy. Applications to vision and molecular prediction show how domain-specific coordinates change the resource comparison. An $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ case study quantifies the dimension dependence of quotient-space approximation gains and compares optimized compute frontiers, alongside separate analyses of conformational coverage and correlated-sample precision.

title: Emergent Active-Blob Length Scale Governs the Collapse Transition of Tangentially Driven Polymers
authors: Baptiste Parage, Sara Jabbari-Farouji
abstract: The coil-to-globule transition is a paradigmatic phenomenon in polymer physics and biophysics, in which polymer chains evolve from swollen to globular conformations upon decreasing solvent quality. At equilibrium, this transition can be rationalized in terms of a thermal blob length that diverges at the so-called $Θ$ condition, marking the crossover from self-avoiding to globular conformations. How activity modifies this conformational transition and affects the fundamental length scales at play remains poorly understood. Here, we address this question for tangentially driven polymers using Brownian dynamics simulations, systematically varying both intrachain attraction strength and activity. We find that polar activity smears out the crossover from swollen to globular conformations. Between self-avoiding and $Θ$ conditions, activity dominates by introducing an emergent folding length scale, which acts as an active blob length. In this regime, we demonstrate that the ratio of thermal to active length scales provides a new scaling variable that leads to a universal master curve for active polymer collapse.

title: Fates of Exact Finite-$N$ First-Order Transitions: Coherent Suppression versus Spectral-Collapse Termination
authors: Jiong Li, Li-Wei Duan, Qing-Hu Chen, Hai-Qing Lin
abstract: Symmetry-protected ground-state crossings can produce exact first-order transitions (FOTs) even at finite $N$, in contrast to continuous transitions governed by soft-mode criticality. We establish exact Juddian ground-state crossings for arbitrary finite $N$ in the one- and two-photon anisotropic Dicke models and identify a common two-channel structure: the eigenvalues of the coupling matrix set the local normal-state instability thresholds, whereas its determinant fixes the exact crossing. Despite this common structure, the resulting FOTs have distinct fates determined by the bosonic response. In the one-photon model, the overlap between coherent Juddian branches vanishes in the thermodynamic or infinite frequency-ratio limits, asymptotically suppressing the FOT cusp. In the two-photon model, squeezed Juddian states lose normalizability at spectral collapse, thereby terminating the physical FOT line at finite $N$. Although the cusp strength tends to zero as the endpoint is approached, the terminating FOT retains a collective spectral signature: the different-parity gap is predicted to close with an $N$-dependent exponent $μ_N=(2N+3)/4$, one greater than the cusp termination exponent. By contrast, the same-parity soft mode retains $N$-independent square-root scaling and governs the critical response. Thus spectral collapse can terminate an exact finite-$N$ FOT while preserving its collective imprint in the parity-resolved spectrum.

title: How Much Do $\ell_1$ Attacks Need Concentrated Perturbations?
authors: Melika Shirian, Kianoosh Vadaei, Arshia Hemmat
abstract: A global $\ell_1$ budget limits how much an adversary may change an image, not how that change is distributed. We ask how much of an $\ell_1$ attack's observed success remains when large coordinate changes are restricted. We add a per-coordinate cap to the budget, enforce the joint constraint by exact in-loop projection, and sweep the cap for APGD-$\ell_1$, SLIDE, and FMN-$\ell_1$ without altering their objectives. Across 18 standard-model settings, caps of at most $32/255$ retain a median $97\%$ of attack success relative to each method's native uncapped baseline, while median peak magnitude falls by $80\%$ and median effective support nearly triples. At matched realized $\ell_1$, capped perturbations remain structurally distinct; separate ImageNet comparisons also show lower LPIPS and DISTS at selected caps. Direct in-loop constrained optimization preserves up to $88$ percentage points more attack success than post-hoc clipping, highlighting the importance of constraint enforcement. Suitable caps nevertheless vary across attacks and models, and adversarially trained classifiers exhibit more heterogeneous concentration sensitivity. These results establish perturbation concentration as a complementary, model- and attack-dependent axis of $\ell_1$ attack evaluation.

title: Bidirectional Path Integral Monte Carlo Simulation of Quantum Circuits
authors: Luis Paulo Santos, Thomas Bashford-Rogers
abstract: We propose an approximate classical algorithm for estimating quantum circuits' transition amplitudes, $\langle Ψ_f | \hat{U} | Ψ_0 \rangle$, based on Monte Carlo sums over bidirectionally sampled Feynman paths. The algorithm generates Feynman paths, i.e., sequences of intermediate computational basis states, by combining information from random walks initiated at both the input and output states, $Ψ_0$ and $Ψ_f$, respectively. It further combines this bidirectional approach with Multiple Importance Sampling, a powerful variance reduction technique that avoids variance peaks caused by divisions by the very low sampling probabilities associated with hard to reach paths. Empirical data demonstrate the superior convergence rate exhibited by the bidirectional algorithm over a unidirectional, forward-only sampling approach. This superiority is due to the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm in finding and weighting paths with non-zero amplitude in an extremely sparse path space. Sum of paths algorithms exhibit very favourable space complexity. Monte Carlo replaces exhaustive enumeration of the exponentially large path space by stochastic sampling, the computational cost being determined by the variance of the estimator. This work demonstrates these two features by presenting results on very large quantum circuits, with up to 4096 qubits.

title: Testing TLS 1.3 PQC on constrained devices and microcontrollers
authors: Olivier Gillot, William J. Buchanan, Callum Turino
abstract: The UK, EU and US governments have set timelines for post-quantum cryptography migration of critical systems, with deadlines ranging from 2028 to 2035. This paper focuses on IoT-class devices and microcontrollers and the viability of using PQC to connect these devices in secure TLS 1.3 connections. Using wolfSSL, we benchmark a 36-combination TLS 1.3 algorithm matrix, pairing ML-KEM-512/768/1024 and X25519/ECC P-256 key exchange with ML-DSA-44/65/87, Ed25519, ECDSA, and RSA-PSS authentication, across four devices (Raspberry Pi Pico W & Pico 2 W, ESP32, and a Raspberry Pi Zero), measuring both handshake latency and energy consumption. We found that in capable devices, all choices in the TLS matrix gave similar results, but that in IoT-class devices, PQC performance is highly implementation- and architecture-dependent: the common assumption that elliptic-curve key exchange must be cheaper than post-quantum lattice-based key exchange does not hold in this wolfSSL-based implementation, where the best full-PQC combination (ML-KEM-512 + ML-DSA-44) completes TLS handshakes 41% faster than the equivalent classical-modern pairing (X25519 + RSA-PSS) on the Pico W (up to 2.12x as energy-efficient, depending on the paired authentication algorithm), and 8.9x faster on the ESP32. Full-PQC, ML-KEM-512/ML-DSA-44, is not only possible but energy-competitive with or superior to Hybrid or Elliptic Curve alternatives on the most constrained devices, though ML-DSA's variable signing time means applications with strict latency-predictability budgets must accept this variance as the cost of full quantum-safe authentication. We further show that the IETF's draft-specified X25519+ML-KEM-768 hybrid incurs approximately the combined cost of its two components, rather than offering a performance compromise, making pure ML-KEM the more practical choice on hardware lacking Curve25519 assembly support.

title: CrystalAR: Autoregressive Modeling for Symmetric Crystal Generation
authors: Ziqiao Meng, Rongsheng Chen, Zhi Zheng, Nikita Kazeev, Zhenkun Wang, Andrey Ustyuzhanin, Wee Sun Lee
abstract: Deep generative modeling has achieved remarkable progress in crystal generation. Given the rich symmetries inherent in crystalline structures, recent work has sought to explicitly incorporate space-group symmetry into generative models, enabling more effective exploration of novel symmetry templates. Yet introducing symmetry templates increases the combinatorial complexity of stoichiometric relationships between atomic species and crystallographic sites, while creating a fundamental tension between flexible exploration of discrete crystallographic templates and faithful realization of these templates as continuous three-dimensional structures. To address these challenges, we propose CrystalAR, a unified autoregressive framework that models Wyckoff symmetry templates and complete crystal structures within a single generative sequence. Specifically, CrystalAR reformulates continuous coordinate generation as a symmetry-conditioned hierarchy of discrete spatial localization decisions, autoregressively refining the positions of all symmetry-inequivalent sites across resolution levels while jointly modeling their spatial configuration within each level. This discrete hierarchical formulation further enables constraint-aware search over both crystallographic templates and geometric realizations. As a result, CrystalAR retains strong symmetry-template generation capability while achieving competitive de novo generation performance and template-free crystal structure prediction (CSP) accuracy. These results suggest that symmetry-template generation can be retained alongside broadly competitive de novo generation performance and competitive CSP without reliance on symmetry templates retrieved from prior data, providing a promising alternative paradigm for symmetry-preserving crystal generation.

title: PixelSR: Pixel-Space Orthogonal Flow Decoupling for Real-World Image Super-Resolution
authors: Xiang Lv, Kai Zhao, Qiang Wang, Qiao Mo, Chao Zhou, Mingwen Shao
abstract: Latent diffusion models have recently achieved remarkable progress in Real-world Image Super-Resolution (Real-SR). However, existing methods consistently exhibit a persistent seesaw effect: enhancing perceptual realism compromises structural fidelity. This effect, we argue, is not intrinsic to diffusion models, but largely stems from the architectural constraints of prevailing two-stage frameworks. To address this challenge, we propose PixelSR, a novel single-stage Pixel Diffusion Transformer for Real-SR that operates directly in pixel space. Specifically, PixelSR consists of two core designs: Pixel-space Conditional Diffusion and Orthogonal Flow Decoupling. The former establishes an effective pixel-space restoration framework by integrating spatially aligned LR conditioning, visual semantic guidance, and lightweight texture refinement, thereby bypassing VAE compression and enabling end-to-end optimization directly in RGB space. Complementarily, the latter decomposes the asymmetric flow target into a low-rank semantic component and a noise-free orthogonal texture component. By routing these components to specialized branches, it achieves decoupled optimization with reduced mutual interference. Benefiting from these designs, our PixelSR restores perceptually realistic details while faithfully preserving structural content. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that PixelSR not only achieves competitive performance, but also effectively mitigates the fidelity--realism seesaw effect.

title: Revealing Inter-Channel Modality Discriminability: Channel Selective Interaction Fusion Network for Optical-SAR Object Detection
authors: Haojie Li, Yuanfei Huang, Lingfei Song, Jia Li, Lizhi Wang
abstract: Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) and optical imagery provide complementary structural and appearance information for remote sensing object detection. However, substantial cross-modal discrepancies and indiscriminate channel interaction inevitably introduce redundant or conflicting features. Since different feature channels encode heterogeneous semantic information and contribute unequally to cross-modal fusion, selectively highlighting task-relevant channels while suppressing redundant ones is essential. To address this issue, we propose the Channel Selective Interaction Fusion Network (CSIF-Net), which performs selective channel-level cross-modal interaction. CSIF-Net first employs a frequency decomposition module to construct frequency-aware SAR inputs, facilitating the separation of structural information from noise-related responses. It then models cross-modal channel relationships through a cross-attention channel selection module and dynamically partitions the features into shared and modality-specific components. Finally, a dual-branch fusion module performs cross-modal interaction and channel realignment for shared features while independently enhancing SAR-specific features, thereby exploiting complementary information and suppressing modality interference. Extensive experiments on the OGSOD 1.0 and M4-SAR datasets demonstrate that CSIF-Net achieves state-of-the-art performance in both horizontal and oriented object detection, surpassing the existing methods by 4.01% and 3.18% gains, respectively.

title: Detection of Memorization in Diffusion Models Through Thermodynamic Singularity
authors: Iljung Kim, Kangwoo Park, Yung-Kyun Noh, Daniel D. Lee
abstract: In diffusion models, proper distributional learning entails reversing a diffusion process over underlying density functions, whereas a key failure is memorization, in which the reverse process instead learns diffusion from individual training samples. We provide an analytical characterization of such memorized reverse processes, along with a criterion that detects the associated thermodynamic singularity. The proposed criterion reliably distinguishes between properly learned and memorizing networks across a range of neural network models designed to promote or mitigate memorization.

title: Market Regime-Based Multi-Asset Portfolio Optimization Using Nested Clustered Optimization for Tactical Asset Allocation
authors: Supriadi, Bambang Siswoyo
abstract: We propose a regime-aware tactical asset allocation (TAA) framework integrating market regime detection with Nested Clustered Optimization (NCO) for multi-asset portfolio construction. The central hypothesis is that incorporating market regime information into the NCO pipeline, specifically at the stages of covariance estimation, hierarchical clustering, and weight optimization, yields portfolios with improved risk-adjusted performance and reduced downside risk relative to regime-agnostic baselines. Market regimes (Bullish, Sideways/Neutral, Bearish) are detected using a Gaussian Hidden Markov Model (HMM) fitted exclusively on information available up to each decision point, thereby preventing look-ahead bias. Regime-conditional covariance matrices and clustering structures parameterize NCO at each rebalancing event. An adaptive rebalancing rule, triggered by regime transitions or material changes in optimal weights, replaces fixed-calendar rebalancing. The framework is evaluated on a heterogeneous monthly multi-asset universe comprising Indonesian government bonds (SBN), the LQ45 equity index, gold (IDR-denominated), foreign exchange (CNY/IDR), and Bitcoin/IDR (BTC). Out-of-sample performance is assessed via rolling walk-forward backtesting. Benchmarks include equal-weight (1/N), buy-and-hold, standard NCO without regime awareness, minimum variance, hierarchical risk parity (HRP), and a rule-based regime strategy. Performance metrics include cumulative return, annualized Sharpe ratio, Sortino ratio, maximum drawdown, Calmar ratio, turnover, and net-of-cost returns. Statistical significance is assessed using the Jobson-Korkie test. The empirical analysis indicates that the proposed regime-aware TAA framework successfully limits tail risk, achieving a maximum drawdown of 4.44% and demonstrating the utility of HMM-based regime detection in multi-asset risk management.

title: Multimode Parametric Amplifier for K-Band Quantum Measurements
authors: Chulwoo Ahn, Vladimir Manucharyan
abstract: We demonstrate K-band nondegenerate three-wave-mixing amplification in a multimode resonator comprising an array of 500 SNAILs. Pairing K-band signal modes with lower-frequency internal idler modes enables 20 dB of gain continuously from 19.6 to 25.6 GHz with pump frequencies below 32.2 GHz. At 20 dB gain, the 3-dB bandwidth ranges from 2.6 to 11.7 MHz, and the input-referred 1-dB compression power reaches -100.9 dBm. In the 20-22 GHz band, the average added noise is 0.73 quanta. A two-mode nondegenerate parametric amplification model describes the measured gain response and gain-bandwidth behavior, while a multimode Kerr model captures the overall compression scale. Our amplifier provides a practical solution for implementing a state-of-the-art readout of superconducting qubits in the K-band.

title: Sharp boundedness criteria for nonnegative kernels on regular curves in the Heisenberg group
authors: Lingxiao Zhang
abstract: In this paper we study singular integrals associated with the nonnegative kernels \[ K_α(x,y,z)=\frac{|z|^{α/2}}{\|(x,y,z)\|^{α+1}}, \qquad α>0, \] in the first Heisenberg group $\mathbb H$, where $\|\cdot\|$ denotes the Korányi norm. This family was introduced by Chousionis and Li. We first show that there exists a compact $1$-Ahlfors regular horizontal $C^1$ curve $E\subset\mathbb H$ such that the singular integrals associated with $K_α$ are unbounded on $L^2(E)$ for every $0<α<4$. This extends the counterexamples of Chousionis, Li and Zhang from $0<α<2$ to the full range $0<α<4$. Combined with the boundedness theorem of Fässler and Orponen for $α\ge4$, our result determines the exact range of exponents for boundedness on every $1$-Ahlfors regular curve. We also consider the more general kernels \[ K_Φ(p)=\frac{1}{\|p\|} Φ\!\left(\frac{|z|^{1/2}}{\|p\|}\right), \qquad p=(x,y,z)\neq0, \] where $Φ:[0,1]\to[0,\infty)$ is continuous and nondecreasing, with $Φ(0)=0$. We show that the associated singular integral is $L^2$-bounded on every $1$-Ahlfors regular curve if and only if $Φ(u)=O(u^4)$ as $u\to0$. When this condition fails, we construct a compact $1$-Ahlfors regular horizontal $C^1$ curve on which the operator is unbounded. The curves in both constructions can be chosen as horizontal lifts of planar $C^1$ graphs with arbitrarily small slope.

title: Tracing Recurrent and Emergent Hallucination Patterns in Decomposed Text-to-SQL Generation
authors: Hayden Moore, Abhinav Verma, Anshuman Dutt
abstract: Large language models can achieve strong Text-to-SQL benchmark performance while still producing schema and query-logic errors. Most evaluations characterize such failures only in the final generated query, making it difficult to determine whether a related error was also observed in an earlier, simpler step or appears only at the final stage. We present a drill-down evaluation framework that decomposes Text-to-SQL queries into progressively more complex executable sub-queries and corresponding natural-language questions, allowing rule-based hallucination categories to be examined across a generation path. We distinguish recurrent hallucinations, in which the same rule-based category is observed in an earlier step and again in the final query, from emergent hallucinations, in which the category is observed at the final step without an earlier detection in the same path. Across five LLMs evaluated on an expanded BIRD-mini benchmark, several categories show appreciable recurrence probabilities, while clause abuse shows comparatively higher conditional emergence. Under the conversational-history condition, recurrence probabilities are generally higher and emergence probabilities are generally lower. These observations indicate that the two conditional measures do not move uniformly in the same direction under additional context and motivate trajectory-level analysis in addition to final-output evaluation. Code and evaluation artifacts are available in the project repository. https://github.com/HaydenMM/bird-mini-drilldown

title: Maximal ranks of free abelian subgroups of generalized cactus groups associated with finite Coxeter systems
authors: Jan Kim, Junseok Kim
abstract: We determine the maximum ranks of free abelian subgroups of generalized cactus groups associated with finite Coxeter systems. To obtain the upper bounds, we use the cubical flat torus theorem of Wise and Woodhouse. We then verify the sharpness of these upper bounds by constructing free abelian subgroups of the corresponding ranks. Our result shows that the maximal ranks of free abelian subgroups of ordinary cactus groups can be larger than conjectured by Genevois. As an application, we show that these groups are not quasi-isometric to any right-angled Artin group unless they are virtually free abelian.

title: Nanophotonic Extreme Ultraviolet Polarimeter
authors: Anna Kulter, Lorenz Weiß, David J. Grafinger, Alexander Sagar Grossek, Rodolfo Previdi, Martin Schultze, Marcus Ossiander
abstract: Nanophotonic engineering has revolutionized how we manipulate the polarization of visible light. Here, we extend such control to extreme ultraviolet radiation, the spectral region of attosecond science and semiconductor lithography, where transmissive optical elements are lacking. We implement channel waveguides that restrict incident 41-nm-wavelength light to a few modes with defined spatial profiles and propagation constants. By designing the propagation-length-dependent interference of two eigenmodes, we achieve polarization-dependent forward scattering, which we exploit to create a transmissive nanophotonic analyzer that resolves the polarization axis and spectrum of extreme ultraviolet light from a single measurement. With a 0.9°-sensitivity for polarization rotations in a 1-second measurement and single-shot capability, the device opens new experimental opportunities in ultrafast magneto-optic spectroscopy and at accelerator-based light sources.

title: Knowledge as Code
authors: Martin Monperrus
abstract: For millennia, knowledge has been carried by language, and large language models still put language at the center. Yet the coding agents built on these models mostly write code. This paper is a contribution to epistemology, which asks what kind of knowledge code is and how it is obtained. We define knowledge as code as knowledge written in a programming language or in a machine-parsable data format, whose validity can be checked by executing it. We define thirteen epistemic properties of knowledge media and show that code is the first medium to have all of them. We distinguish two ways in which knowledge enters code, encoding and learning by execution, where code is both the experiment and the record of its result. Agents make learning by execution observable, since their trajectories record every probe, observation and line of code they keep. Code is thus not only a tool of knowledge work but a knowledge medium in its own right, the first that can check what it holds.

title: A Principled Optimal Transport Framework for Frame Selection in Long Video Understanding
authors: Ziwei Zhao, Yuhang Liu
abstract: Long-video understanding with multimodal LLMs is fundamentally constrained by the mismatch between video length and the model's limited visual context budget, making frame selection essential for practical reasoning. Existing query-aware methods typically rely on heuristic pipelines: they assign one-dimensional query-conditioned scores to frames and then apply sampling, ranking, or extraction rules to form the final subset. While effective in practice, such methods are generally not derived from an explicit optimization objective and struggle to capture the heterogeneous evidence required for complex reasoning. In this paper, we revisit long-video frame selection from a principled optimization perspective. We formulate it as a structured evidence-allocation problem and propose OTFS, an optimal transport framework that maps multiple evidence sources onto video frames. To reflect the asymmetry of this problem---important evidence should be preserved, whereas redundant frames need not absorb mass---we instantiate this view with a semi-unbalanced entropic optimal transport objective and an efficient solver, OTFS-Sinkhorn. Combined with an exact dynamic program for coverage-aware subset extraction, OTFS yields a practical two-stage training-free pipeline. We further show that, in the single-source case, our formulation induces a Gibbs-type distribution over frames, making Q-Frame's temperature-scaled distribution a special case of our framework while also providing a broader perspective for understanding related prior methods.
